Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Gerald Hoffmann is a 67-year-old married school principal of German-American heritage who presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. He arrived punctually, dressed with the careful formality one might expect of a man who has spent decades setting the tone for an institution, though his posture carried a fatigue that seemed to predate the appointment itself.

The collision occurred on a Tuesday morning in late autumn when Gerald was driving to school along a route he had taken for eleven years. A delivery truck ran a red light at speed and struck the driver's side of his sedan. The impact was immediate and total — the shriek of metal, the implosion of glass, the sickening lurch of the car being spun across two lanes. Gerald has described the sound as something that did not seem to belong in the world, a crash so loud and sudden that his body registered it before his mind could. He was conscious throughout, pinned briefly by the crumpled door frame, and in those minutes he was certain he was dying. Paramedics reported he was shouting when they arrived, though Gerald has no memory of this. He sustained fractured ribs, a lacerated forearm, and a concussion. He was discharged from hospital within five days.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald found that the event would not settle into the past. His memories did not behave like memories. When images returned — particularly the sight of cars approaching intersections, or photographs of accident scenes glimpsed on a news feed — they did not feel like recollections. They felt like the present. He would be standing in his kitchen and the truck would be hitting him again, the force of it still in his chest. He has described these episodes with a kind of bewildered frustration: he knows, intellectually, that he is in his kitchen, but the knowledge does not help. The experience itself resists being put into language. When asked directly to describe what happened, he often trails off, gesturing vaguely, as though the event exists in a register that words cannot reach — only sensation, only image, only the film that runs and runs.

Loud noises became a particular source of dread. At school, where Gerald has spent most of his professional life managing the controlled chaos of several hundred children, the ordinary sounds of an institution — a door slamming in a corridor, students shouting across a courtyard, the clatter of a dropped tray in the cafeteria — began to feel intolerable. He had come to believe, with a certainty he could not fully justify, that the world was genuinely and pervasively dangerous, and that his previous sense of safety had simply been ignorance. He started arriving late and leaving early, finding reasons to conduct his work remotely when possible. Over three months, his absences became noticeable enough that his deputy principal raised the matter with him directly — a conversation Gerald found humiliating, and which confirmed his private fear that he had permanently changed for the worse, that the man who had run that school with confidence and steadiness was simply gone.

At home, evenings had become their own ordeal. He could not relax, even in the stillness of the house he has shared with his wife for thirty-four years. Sleep came reluctantly and left early. When something ran late — a family member not yet home at the expected hour, a phone call that went unanswered — he found himself convinced that disaster was unfolding, that the delay meant something terrible had happened. He began eating in the evenings in a way that felt less like appetite and more like filling a space, and he was aware that this, too, was not who he had been. He forced himself, during the days, to think only of what was good and manageable, consciously steering his attention away from anything dark — a discipline that cost him considerable energy and left him exhausted.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a quiet remark from his wife, who told him one evening that she felt she was living with someone who was waiting for the next catastrophe. He had sat with that for several days. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that she is right.
